Making the Back Seat Bearable

Factory pillion seats are often an afterthought — thin, narrow, and uncomfortable after 30 minutes. If you want your passenger to enjoy touring rather than endure it, investing in pillion comfort upgrades is essential. The good news is that relatively modest investments can dramatically improve the rear riding experience.

Seat Upgrades

The seat is the most impactful upgrade. Options range from simple bolt-on solutions to fully custom seats:

  • Gel seat pads — Products like AirHawk Air Pad or Wild Ass cushion sit on top of the existing seat. Air cells distribute pressure and reduce numbness. The cheapest and easiest upgrade at around forty to sixty pounds.
  • Custom pillion seats — Companies like Corbin and Sargent create seats with better foam density, wider bases, and improved shapes. Expensive but transformative for regular pillion touring.
  • Sheepskin covers — A genuine sheepskin cover adds cushioning and breathability. They look slightly eccentric but the comfort improvement is genuine.

Backrests

A backrest gives the pillion something to lean against under acceleration and prevents them sliding backward on the seat. Options include dedicated passenger backrests that bolt to the subframe, top boxes that double as backrests, and adjustable systems that fold away when not carrying a passenger. A top box with a comfortable pad is the most practical solution as it provides luggage space and a backrest simultaneously.

Footpeg Upgrades

Standard pillion footpegs are often small and poorly positioned. Wider aftermarket pegs reduce pressure points on the soles and allow the pillion to shift their feet for comfort. Lowering kits reposition the pegs downward, reducing knee angle for taller passengers. Rubber-mounted pegs reduce vibration transmitted through the feet.

Wind Protection

Pillions sit higher and more exposed than riders. If your bike has a tall screen that protects you but deflects turbulence onto your pillion, consider a different screen height or profile. Some manufacturers offer pillion-specific wind deflectors that attach to the rear of the bike.

Heating and Electronics

Heated seat — Aftermarket heated seat pads plug into the bike's 12V system. A warm seat on a cold morning is deeply appreciated by pillions.

Intercom — A Bluetooth intercom system in the pillion's helmet is essential. Communication prevents frustration and improves safety.

Entertainment — Some intercom systems let the pillion listen to music or podcasts independently. On long motorway stretches, this dramatically reduces boredom.

Ask your pillion what bothers them most about riding as a passenger. The answer might surprise you — it could be wind noise, seat pressure, cold feet, or simply boredom. Address their specific complaint and you both enjoy touring more.
keyTakeaways: The seat is the highest-impact upgrade, from a cheap gel pad to a custom Corbin or Sargent unit.
A backrest, often a top box with a pad, stops the pillion sliding back under acceleration.
Wider footpegs and lowering kits reduce pressure points and cramped knees on long days.
An intercom and optional entertainment cut boredom and improve safety on motorway stretches.
Ask your pillion what bothers them most, then target that specific complaint first.

faq.q: What is the cheapest way to improve pillion comfort?
faq.a: A gel or air seat pad such as an AirHawk or Wild Ass cushion is the cheapest and easiest upgrade, sitting on top of the existing seat for around forty to sixty pounds. The air cells distribute pressure and reduce numbness on long days. A sheepskin cover is another inexpensive option that adds cushioning and breathability, if you can accept the eccentric look.

faq.q: Do I need a backrest for my pillion?
faq.a: A backrest greatly improves comfort by giving the pillion something to lean against under acceleration and stopping them sliding backward. The most practical solution is a top box fitted with a comfortable pad, which provides luggage space and a backrest at once. Dedicated bolt-on passenger backrests are also available, and some fold away when you ride solo.

faq.q: How can I reduce pillion boredom on long rides?
faq.a: A Bluetooth intercom is the key upgrade, letting rider and pillion talk, which prevents frustration and improves safety. Many intercom systems also let the passenger listen to music or podcasts independently, which dramatically reduces boredom on long motorway stretches. Comfortable seating and regular stops for a stretch and a chat also keep morale high on a long day.

faq.q: Should I change the screen for my pillion?
faq.a: Possibly. Pillions sit higher and more exposed than the rider, so a tall screen that protects you may deflect turbulent air straight onto your passenger. If they complain of buffeting, experiment with a different screen height or profile, or fit a pillion-specific wind deflector that attaches to the rear of the bike. Getting the airflow right off the passenger makes a big difference to comfort.
